Name: analogical_transfer_gate
Title: Solved It Once, Solving It Again: An Internal Analogy Gate That Determines Whether Reasoning Models Reuse a Worked Example or Re-Derive From Scratch
Short Hypothesis: Narrowly scoped setting: a fully-worked solution to a problem is placed in-context IMMEDIATELY BEFORE a target that is structurally identical but differs only in surface details (numbers, cover story, variable names). We hypothesize that reasoning models frequently FAIL to reuse the just-seen method -- re-deriving from scratch and wasting a large number of tokens -- and that, mirroring human analogical transfer, this failure is modulated by surface vs. structural similarity. The single falsifiable mechanistic claim: at the token boundary where the target begins (before any target reasoning token), the residual stream carries a linearly-decodable 'analogy-gate' signal that predicts reuse vs. re-derivation, that is distinct from a raw target-difficulty signal and from surface lexical overlap, and that causally controls the decision -- steering it flips the model between reuse and re-derivation. This is not generic in-context learning (the target is a new instance requiring the same method, not a demonstration to imitate token-for-token), not within-single-problem overthinking, and not static task-vector reuse; it is a dynamic, onset-specific decision to transfer or not. Falsifier: the onset representation predicts only difficulty, or steering changes length without changing reuse behavior.
Related Work: Three previously-disconnected lines, separated by what each addresses and the delta we add. (1) Behavioral analogical transfer in cognitive science (Structure-Mapping Theory; 'Transfer Between Analogies' 1995; 'A model of retrieval in problem solving' 1989; 'A theory of relation learning and cross-domain generalization' 2022) documents that humans reuse solutions to structurally-similar problems, gated by surface vs. structural similarity -- but says nothing about LLMs or token cost. (2) Mechanistic circuit/computation reuse and steering (Circuit Component Reuse Across Tasks 2023; Shared Circuits for Sequence Continuation 2023; Extrapolation by Association 2025; task-vector extraction work) shows internal components are shared across tasks and task identity can be read from activations -- but studies STATIC shared components, not the dynamic in-context decision to transfer a just-seen worked solution, and offers no efficiency measurement. (3) Systems-level activation/KV caching (LLMCache, AttMemo, KVShare 2023-2025) reuses computation EXTERNALLY without asking whether the model itself recognizes the analogy. Our delta against all three: we pose the behavioral question none of them do -- does a reasoning model reuse its OWN just-seen worked solution on a new instance of the same problem, or wastefully re-derive, and how many tokens does that cost -- and then locate and causally steer an onset-specific analogy gate distinct from static task vectors and from a scalar difficulty probe. This differs from our prior proposals, which concern within-single-problem overthinking.
Abstract: Humans who have just solved a problem reuse the method when they encounter a structurally identical one, thinking far less the second time. We ask whether reasoning language models do the same in the specific, common setting where a worked example is appended immediately before a new instance -- as happens in assistants with few-shot exemplars, code agents, and tutoring systems. We present a reasoning model with a fully-worked solution, then a target that is structurally identical but differs in surface details, and measure whether it transfers the method (short, reuse-style reasoning) or re-derives from scratch (long, redundant reasoning). We hypothesize that models frequently fail to transfer, wasting tokens -- a concrete inference cost and latency penalty -- and that, mirroring human analogy, transfer succeeds more with high surface similarity and fails when only deep structure is shared. Across GSM8K, MATH500, and templated algorithmic word problems on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we quantify a transfer-failure rate and its surface-vs-structure modulation with difficulty-, length-, and lexical-overlap-matched controls. We then test a falsifiable mechanistic account: at the token boundary where the target begins, the residual stream linearly encodes an analogy-gate signal predicting reuse vs. re-derivation, separable from difficulty and surface overlap. We localize it via activation patching, causally steer it to flip behavior with specificity controls (a tempting but structurally-different distractor must not induce harmful reuse), and turn it into a training-free intervention that induces reuse when a valid analog is present, cutting tokens at equal accuracy. The result reframes a slice of overthinking as steerable analogical-transfer failure with direct prompt-design and inference-routing implications.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — Reasoning models frequently fail to transfer a just-seen worked solution to a structurally identical target): The behavioral test. Data: constructed analog pairs. Draw 250 seed problems from GSM8K, MATH500, and templated algorithmic word problems with well-defined solution methods; for each seed generate (a) a surface-similar structural analog (same method, similar cover story, different numbers), (b) a structure-only analog (same method, different cover story/domain), and (c) a surface-similar structurally-different distractor (similar wording, different method). Verify structural equivalence via solution-step-template matching plus an LLM-judge check and a 150-pair human spot-check. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B, 7B, 14B and Qwen3-8B, frozen, inference only; temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, max 16384 tokens, 3 seeds. Systems compared, per condition: [worked analog + target] vs [target alone] vs [irrelevant worked solution + target]. Decisive metric: transfer-failure rate — the fraction of structural-analog trials whose target reasoning-token count is not substantially reduced (< 20% below the target-alone baseline) despite retained accuracy. Secondary: mean token reduction and accuracy per condition (surface-similar vs structure-only vs distractor), and whether the distractor induces harmful reuse (accuracy drop). Convincing result: transfer-failure rate >= 40% overall with a real opportunity cost (surface-similar analogs cut tokens by >= 25% at retained accuracy when transfer does occur), establishing that models leave substantial savings on the table. Indecision band: a transfer-failure rate in [20%, 40%) means failure is real but modest; below 20% (models almost always transfer) means there is little phenomenon to explain and the mechanistic program is unmotivated. Negative result (models reliably transfer, near-zero failure) would refute the premise.

Experiment 2 (H2 — An analogy-gate signal at target onset linearly predicts transfer vs re-derivation, separable from difficulty): Tests the decodable gate. Data: ~4000 [worked analog + target] boundary states from Experiment 1 labeled transfer vs re-derive, 1200 held-out from disjoint seeds. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (primary), 1.5B and 14B, frozen; only linear probes trained. Method: at the token boundary where the target begins (after the worked example, before any target reasoning token) fit per-layer linear probes to predict transfer vs re-derivation. Systems compared: the analogy-gate probe vs (i) a difficulty probe trained on target pass-rate, (ii) a surface-similarity feature baseline, (iii) prior-text bag-of-words. Decisive metric: transfer-prediction AUROC on held-out seeds. Secondary: partial correlation with the transfer label after removing difficulty and surface overlap, and principal angle between the gate and difficulty directions. Convincing result: AUROC >= 0.75 at some layer, partial correlation >= 0.25 after removing difficulty and surface overlap, and principal angle >= 30 degrees from the difficulty direction. Indecision band: AUROC in [0.65, 0.75) or principal angle in [15, 30) degrees means the gate is real but largely reducible to difficulty/surface features — reported as an entangled correlate; AUROC < 0.65 means no distinct gate and H2 fails. Negative result would leave transfer failure as a behavioral fact without an internal decision variable.

Experiment 3 (H3 — Patching the analogy-recognition state causally switches reuse vs re-derivation): Tests causal carry of the gate. Data: 300 matched pairs sharing the same target and method but differing in analog type (surface-similar transfer-inducing vs structure-only re-derivation). Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; intervention is activation patching of the target-boundary state at candidate layers from the surface-similar context into the structure-only context and vice versa. Systems compared: real patch vs matched-random-direction patch of equal norm; off-target accuracy control. Decisive metric: the fraction of trials that switch to reuse (token drop plus method-matched solution) under patching. Convincing result: patching flips >= 40% of re-derivation trials to reuse, exceeding the random-direction control by >= 25 points, with off-target accuracy unchanged (< 5 points). Indecision band: a flip rate in [20%, 40%) or margin over random < 25 points is weak causal evidence; below 20% means the boundary state is not the causal gate. Negative result would leave the gate correlational.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Steering the gate induces reuse when a valid analog is present, with specificity): The steering test. Data: held-out [surface-similar analog + target] and [distractor + target] trials. Model: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and 14B, frozen; intervention is steering along the analogy-gate direction (difference-of-means of transfer vs re-derivation boundary states); dose-response swept; 3 seeds. Systems compared: steer-up (induce reuse) vs steer-down (control) vs no intervention vs matched random direction. Decisive metric: token reduction at retained accuracy on valid-analog trials under steer-up, read jointly with the specificity check that steering does NOT induce harmful reuse of the distractor (accuracy must not drop on distractor trials). Convincing result: steer-up cuts median tokens by >= 20% at accuracy within +/- 1.0 point on valid-analog trials, beats the random control by >= 10 points of token change, and leaves distractor-trial accuracy within +/- 1.0 point (no harmful transfer). Indecision band: a token reduction in [5%, 20%), or a distractor-trial accuracy drop in (1.0, 3.0] points, is a weak/partly-harmful outcome reported as such; a distractor accuracy drop > 3 points means steering forces indiscriminate reuse and fails specificity. Negative result (no token reduction, or reduction only with harmful distractor reuse) would refute the controllable-gate claim.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Training-free efficiency application and generalization): Tests the applied payoff and transfer. Data: GSM8K/MATH500/algorithmic held-out trials where a valid worked analog is in context (detected cheaply by template match); plus cross-domain analogs (a math method reused in a physics word problem). Models: 7B and 14B, frozen; apply gate steering to induce reuse when a valid analog is detected. Systems compared: gate steering vs no intervention vs simple prompting ('reuse the method above'). Decisive metric: tokens-at-equal-accuracy (median token reduction subject to accuracy within noise) over the valid-analog stream. Secondary: whether the probe and steering direction transfer across datasets, scales, and to cross-domain analogs without retraining. Convincing result: gate steering saves >= 15% tokens at accuracy within +/- 1.0 point, matching or beating the prompting baseline, and retains >= two-thirds of its effect across datasets and on cross-domain analogs. Indecision band: token savings in [5%, 15%), or transfer retention in [one-third, two-thirds), is a modest/partial outcome; below those means no practical edge or no transfer (cross-domain transfer being rare, especially at 1.5B, is itself an informative scope result). Negative result would confine the contribution to the mechanistic findings.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The analogy gate may be inseparable from raw difficulty or surface-overlap features, weakening the mechanistic claim; the separability analysis, patching, and distractor-specificity tests directly address this, and a null would still yield a novel behavioral characterization of transfer failure. Constructing clean structural analogs that hold difficulty constant while varying surface similarity is nontrivial; we mitigate with template-based generation and human/LLM verification of structural equivalence. Transfer-success detection relies on token-count and method-match, which are noisy; we use both token-reduction and step-template matching and validate with human spot-checks. Inducing reuse could cause harmful transfer to structurally-different distractors (accuracy loss); the distractor condition and steering-specificity metric quantify this trade-off. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters. Effects and the strength of surface-vs-structure modulation may be model-family and scale specific, and cross-domain transfer may be rare in smaller models (itself an informative result).
